# Comparing Arabic tokenizers — tables for the supervisor

*Generated by `scripts/build_comparative_tables.py` on 2026-10-13 from the result files; do not edit by hand.*

**The question.** A tokenizer cuts text into the pieces a language model reads and writes. We keep everything else
fixed — the base model, the training data, the training steps, the evaluation — and change only the tokenizer, to see
what the tokenizer alone changes. Four tokenizers are compared: the model's **own** (native) tokenizer; **AraRooPat**,
which writes each Arabic word as a root and a pattern; and two ordinary **BPE** tokenizers trained on the same Arabic
text, one with 16 000 pieces and one with 128 000 (about the size of the native ones). Three base models, to see
whether the findings hold for other model families: Qwen3-4B-Base (complete); Llama-3.2-3B (complete); Gemma-3-4B (complete).

**Equal treatment.** Every version goes through the same training: the from-scratch tokenizers first get two stages
that teach the model its new vocabulary on Arabic web text, then all versions get the same final stage on Arabic
instructions answered by one teacher model (Aya-Expanse-32B). Nothing is tuned for one version alone.

**Two kinds of evaluation.** *Writing*: each version answers the same 250 held-out Arabic instructions, and a separate
judge model scores each answer from 1 to 5 (T2). *Recognition*: four multiple-choice benchmarks, where the model
only ranks given answers (T3).

**The judge.** Gemma-4-31B judged the earlier results, including the deck of 26 September. Gemma is now one of the base
models, so it cannot stay the main judge. The new main judge is an open model run locally, chosen among candidates
from different companies (gpt-oss-120b from OpenAI and Falcon-H1-34B from TII; a third candidate could not be loaded
and was dropped) by its agreement with a blind human rating; until that rating is complete, every candidate's column
is shown. Main judge: **gpt-oss-120b** — named by rule S4 default on 2026-10-11T06:18:15Z (outputs/experiments/_comparative_tables/judge_selection.json).

**What is pending.** the human rating (51 of 200 answers rated). Pending cells say "pending" — they are never zero. T7 at the end
reads the pre-registered findings across the three base models.


## Qwen3-4B-Base

### T1 — Qwen3-4B-Base: the four tokenizers before any training

*How to read:* one column per tokenizer; each row is a property of the tokenizer alone, measured on fixed Arabic text (no model involved). Arrows say which direction is better where there is one.

|  | native | AraRooPat | BPE-16K | BPE-128K |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| vocabulary size (pieces) | 151 936 | 17 184 | 16 000 | 128 000 |
| pieces per word ↓ (fertility, ArabicText-Large eval texts) | 2.30 | 3.19 | 1.50 | 1.23 |
| characters per piece ↑ (same texts) | 2.55 | 1.82 | 3.89 | 4.75 |
| characters per piece on the free-form reference answers | 2.30 | 1.96 | 2.49 | 2.89 |
| pieces per word of web text (the training pool) | 2.23 | 3.04 | 1.69 | 1.36 |
| unknown-piece rate ↓ | 0.00 % | 0.68 % | 0.00 % | 0.00 % |
| words written without an unknown piece ↑ | 100.0 % | 94.5 % | 100.0 % | 100.0 % |
| text given back exactly after encode → decode: reference answers, character overlap (chrF, 0–100) ↑ | 99.4 | 91.1 | 100.0 | 100.0 |
| the same with the answers' diacritics removed first ↑ | 100.0 | 99.0 | 100.0 | 100.0 |
| single words given back exactly (of 2 000 corpus words) ↑ | 100.0 % | 99.3 % | 100.0 % | 100.0 % |
| roots kept inside one piece, where possible ↑ (root conservation, attainable) | 0.088 | 0.418 | 0.053 | 0.178 |
| share of words whose root can be kept at all (the ceiling) | 88.7 % | 88.5 % | 89.0 % | 88.5 % |
| pieces per morpheme (≈ 1 = cut at morpheme size; > 1 = cut finer) | 1.43 | 2.98 | 1.31 | 1.06 |
| the letter أ written as a choice answer, in pieces | 1 | 3 | 1 | 1 |
| pieces the adaptation never showed the model (stages 1–2) | not applicable (no new pieces) | 4.9 % | 3.1 % | 1.0 % |
| pieces it showed fewer than ten times | not applicable (no new pieces) | 20.3 % | 0.6 % | 3.9 % |

**What it shows.** How differently the four tokenizers cut the same Arabic text. A larger vocabulary cuts words into fewer, longer pieces; AraRooPat cuts every word into a root and a pattern, so it needs more pieces per word.

- AraRooPat's root conservation is high *by construction* on the words it writes as root + pattern; the number is a property of its design, not a measured skill (docs/report.md, the intrinsic metrics).
- A larger vocabulary trained on the same text sees each of its pieces less often during the model's adaptation; the last two rows say how many pieces the two adaptation stages never showed the model, or showed it fewer than ten times (scripts/count_adaptation_tokens.py, over the blocks the stages consumed).
- The native vocabularies are much larger than the from-scratch ones (see the first row); BPE-128K is the from-scratch tokenizer of native size.

*Source:* outputs/experiments/_comparative_tables/m5/tokenizer_basics.json (scripts/measure_tokenizer_basics.py) and each arm's intrinsic_metrics.json (the pipeline's intrinsic step)

Only questions that no version had to cut for length are counted, so every version sees the same questions.

### T3c — Qwen3-4B-Base: letter-fair recognition (a proposal, applied to nothing)

*How to read:* the same exam questions asked four times with the answer letters rotated (أ ب ج د moved round), and each question decided by the average over the four. This removes a model's taste for one letter. The 'أ gap' is the difference on the questions whose right answer carries the letter أ in the ordinary order, where AraRooPat lost most.

|  | Arabic exams: letter-fair accuracy | translated MMLU: letter-fair accuracy | Arabic exams: difference to BPE-16K, letter-fair | translated MMLU: difference to BPE-16K, letter-fair | Arabic exams: أ gap to BPE-16K, ordinary order | translated MMLU: أ gap to BPE-16K, ordinary order |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| native (the model's own) | 0.577 | 0.519 | — | — | — | — |
| AraRooPat (roots and patterns) | 0.522 | 0.469 | −0.001 [−0.030, +0.027] | −0.039 [−0.068, −0.011] | −0.202 [−0.236, −0.169] | −0.149 [−0.180, −0.117] |
| BPE, 16 000 pieces | 0.523 | 0.508 | — | — | — | — |
| BPE, 128 000 pieces | 0.519 | 0.474 | −0.004 [−0.031, +0.024] | −0.034 [−0.059, −0.008] | −0.102 [−0.131, −0.074] | −0.088 [−0.114, −0.062] |
| the model before any training | 0.576 | 0.527 | — | — | — | — |

**What it shows.** That most of AraRooPat's exam deficit comes from how it scores the letter أ, not from the questions: once the letters are rotated, the Arabic-exam gap to BPE-16K disappears and a smaller gap remains on the translated MMLU.

- Letter-fair scoring is a proposal recorded in docs/report.md §3.11–§3.13; no headline number of the campaign uses it.

*Source:* qwen_native_vs_araroopat/_letter_slot/letter_slot_bpe128k.json (scripts/mcq_letter_slot.py; 1 000-question subsets)

### T4 — Qwen3-4B-Base: how long the model takes to answer under each tokenizer

*How to read:* every version answers the same 250 instructions one at a time on an otherwise idle GPU, under the evaluation's own rules; the multiple-choice rows score the same 500 questions per benchmark. Fewer pieces per character usually means fewer steps per answer.

|  | seconds per answer (median, one at a time) | milliseconds per 100 characters written ↓ | time to the first piece, ms ↓ | tokenizer's share of answer time | characters per second, 16 at a time ↑ | energy per 1 000 answers, Wh ↓ | multiple-choice: ms per question, Arabic exams ↓ | multiple-choice: ms per question, AlGhafa ↓ | answers identical to the evaluated ones |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| native (the model's own) | 5.12 | 1307 | 36 | 0.0 % | 389 | 310.3 | 155 | 127 | 31 % |
| AraRooPat (roots and patterns) | 5.99 | 1696 | 38 | 0.1 % | 262 | 392.7 | 166 | 140 | 37 % |
| BPE, 16 000 pieces | 4.98 | 1177 | 37 | 0.0 % | 440 | 275.9 | 155 | 122 | 27 % |
| BPE, 128 000 pieces | 3.67 | 1029 | 37 | 0.0 % | 396 | 215.1 | 152 | 122 | 34 % |
| the model before any training | 5.02 | 1321 | 36 | 0.0 % | 288 | 300.8 | 156 | 128 | 36 % |

**What it shows.** The cost of an answer in time and energy, per tokenizer, on the same hardware.

- One answer at a time is the latency a user sees; sixteen at a time is the throughput of the evaluation. Answers differ in length between versions, so 'per 100 characters' is the fair comparison.
- AraRooPat's encoding goes through a morphological analyser in a second process; its share of the answer time is an implementation cost, measured apart in T5.
- 'Answers identical to the evaluated ones' checks that one-at-a-time decoding reproduces the evaluated answers (small differences come from batching arithmetic).

*Source:* each cell's timing_v1.json (scripts/measure_response_time.py)

### T5 — the tokenizers' own speed (processor only, no model)

*How to read:* the same 20 000 Arabic texts, encoded and decoded on the processor; AraRooPat is shown cold (first contact, its analyser starting), warm (the same texts again) and steady (new texts once it is running).

|  | encode, µs per word (one text at a time) ↓ | encode, µs per word (a batch, all cores) ↓ | decode, µs per word ↓ | encode latency of one answer-length text, p95 ms ↓ | whole texts given back exactly (eval texts) | load time, s | memory added by loading, MB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| native Qwen3 | 5.43 | 0.44 | 0.81 | 0.960 | 100.0 % | 0.36 | 127 |
| native Llama-3.2 | 4.91 | 0.43 | 0.83 | 0.910 | 100.0 % | 0.98 | 230 |
| BPE-16K | 3.63 | 0.43 | 0.43 | 0.691 | 100.0 % | 0.03 | 15 |
| BPE-128K | 3.71 | 0.50 | 0.45 | 0.713 | 100.0 % | 0.28 | 78 |
| AraRooPat — cold | 96.1 | not applicable | — | 20.00 | — | 0.25 | 1 186 |
| AraRooPat — warm | 10.2 | not applicable | 2.8 | 2.00 | 0.2 % | — | — |
| AraRooPat — steady | 49.0 | not applicable | — | 27.10 | — | — | — |
| native Gemma-3 | 3.38 | 0.21 | 1.01 | 0.534 | 100.0 % | 1.74 | 329 |

**What it shows.** How much processor time the tokenizer itself costs. The native and BPE tokenizers run compiled code; AraRooPat runs Python plus a morphological analyser in a second process, so its numbers describe this implementation, not the method's limit.

- Measured on a machine also running a GPU training job; the load is recorded in the source file.
- AraRooPat rarely gives a whole text back character for character: decoding re-spaces punctuation, writes Latin-script words as '?' (it has no Latin pieces), and restores a hamza the writer dropped (ا → أ, its canonical spelling, docs/report.md §3.5). Single Arabic words come back exactly far more often (T1).
- AraRooPat's cold row includes its analyser warming up on unseen words; the steady row is new texts once the analyser runs, the case of real use.

*Source:* outputs/experiments/_tokenizer_speed/2026-10-09/speed_v1.json (scripts/measure_tokenizer_speed.py); machine: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8481C CPU @ 2.70GHz

### T6 — Qwen3-4B-Base: the computation each tokenizer makes the model spend

*How to read:* the model body is the same in every column; what changes is the size of the vocabulary tables and how many pieces the same text becomes. Operations are counted for one forward pass; 'G' = 10⁹.

|  | native | AraRooPat | BPE-16K | BPE-128K |
|---|---|---|---|---|

**What it shows.** That the vocabulary tables are a small part of the model at 16 000 pieces and a large part at 128 000 or more, and that a tokenizer cutting text finer makes the model do more work for the same text.

- Stage 3 trains on a fixed number of instruction examples (the same number for every version, set by the mixture), not a fixed number of pieces; its piece count is the examples the run processed × the mixture's mean pieces per example (scripts/count_phase3_tokens.py).

- Equal compute is not equal text: the same 131 M pieces cover very different amounts of Arabic under different tokenizers (the two 'words' rows).

## Llama-3.2-3B

### T1 — Llama-3.2-3B: the four tokenizers before any training

*How to read:* one column per tokenizer; each row is a property of the tokenizer alone, measured on fixed Arabic text (no model involved). Arrows say which direction is better where there is one.

|  | native | AraRooPat | BPE-16K | BPE-128K |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| vocabulary size (pieces) | 128 256 | 17 184 | 16 000 | 128 000 |
| pieces per word ↓ (fertility, ArabicText-Large eval texts) | 2.26 | 3.19 | 1.50 | 1.23 |
| characters per piece ↑ (same texts) | 2.59 | 1.82 | 3.89 | 4.75 |
| characters per piece on the free-form reference answers | 2.36 | 1.96 | 2.49 | 2.89 |
| pieces per word of web text (the training pool) | 2.26 | 3.04 | 1.69 | 1.36 |
| unknown-piece rate ↓ | 0.00 % | 0.68 % | 0.00 % | 0.00 % |
| words written without an unknown piece ↑ | 100.0 % | 94.5 % | 100.0 % | 100.0 % |
| text given back exactly after encode → decode: reference answers, character overlap (chrF, 0–100) ↑ | 100.0 | 91.1 | 100.0 | 100.0 |
| the same with the answers' diacritics removed first ↑ | 100.0 | 99.0 | 100.0 | 100.0 |
| single words given back exactly (of 2 000 corpus words) ↑ | 100.0 % | 99.3 % | 100.0 % | 100.0 % |
| roots kept inside one piece, where possible ↑ (root conservation, attainable) | 0.010 | 0.417 | 0.056 | 0.176 |
| share of words whose root can be kept at all (the ceiling) | 88.5 % | 88.7 % | 88.3 % | 88.3 % |
| pieces per morpheme (≈ 1 = cut at morpheme size; > 1 = cut finer) | 1.89 | 2.98 | 1.31 | 1.06 |
| the letter أ written as a choice answer, in pieces | 1 | 3 | 1 | 1 |
| pieces the adaptation never showed the model (stages 1–2) | not applicable (no new pieces) | 4.9 % | 3.1 % | 1.0 % |
| pieces it showed fewer than ten times | not applicable (no new pieces) | 20.3 % | 0.6 % | 3.9 % |

**What it shows.** How differently the four tokenizers cut the same Arabic text. A larger vocabulary cuts words into fewer, longer pieces; AraRooPat cuts every word into a root and a pattern, so it needs more pieces per word.

- AraRooPat's root conservation is high *by construction* on the words it writes as root + pattern; the number is a property of its design, not a measured skill (docs/report.md, the intrinsic metrics).
- A larger vocabulary trained on the same text sees each of its pieces less often during the model's adaptation; the last two rows say how many pieces the two adaptation stages never showed the model, or showed it fewer than ten times (scripts/count_adaptation_tokens.py, over the blocks the stages consumed).
- The native vocabularies are much larger than the from-scratch ones (see the first row); BPE-128K is the from-scratch tokenizer of native size.

*Source:* outputs/experiments/_comparative_tables/m5/tokenizer_basics.json (scripts/measure_tokenizer_basics.py) and each arm's intrinsic_metrics.json (the pipeline's intrinsic step)

- The distilled versions write at about the teacher's length (mean answer length in T2, continued), and judges tend to prefer longer answers; T2c checks the main comparison on answers of equal length.
- Gemma-4-31B was the judge of the thesis deck of 26 September; it is a Gemma model and Gemma is now one of the base models, so it cannot be the main judge any more (docs/report.md §3.14). Its scores stay here for the record.
- GPT-5.6 judged only the five cells of the 26 September check; it comes from the same company as gpt-oss.

**What it shows.** That the vocabulary tables are a small part of the model at 16 000 pieces and a large part at 128 000 or more, and that a tokenizer cutting text finer makes the model do more work for the same text.

- Stage 3 trains on a fixed number of instruction examples (the same number for every version, set by the mixture), not a fixed number of pieces; its piece count is the examples the run processed × the mixture's mean pieces per example (scripts/count_phase3_tokens.py).
- The native model needs no stages 1 and 2: its vocabulary is the one it was pretrained with.
- Equal compute is not equal text: the same 131 M pieces cover very different amounts of Arabic under different tokenizers (the two 'words' rows).
- Peak memory was not recorded for the Qwen3-4B runs; the Llama and Gemma runs record it (chains/*peak_mem.jsonl).

### T1 — Gemma-3-4B: the four tokenizers before any training

*How to read:* one column per tokenizer; each row is a property of the tokenizer alone, measured on fixed Arabic text (no model involved). Arrows say which direction is better where there is one.

|  | native | AraRooPat | BPE-16K | BPE-128K |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| vocabulary size (pieces) | 262 208 | 17 184 | 16 000 | 128 000 |
| pieces per word ↓ (fertility, ArabicText-Large eval texts) | 2.08 | 3.19 | 1.50 | 1.23 |
| characters per piece ↑ (same texts) | 2.82 | 1.82 | 3.89 | 4.75 |
| characters per piece on the free-form reference answers | 2.59 | 1.96 | 2.49 | 2.89 |
| pieces per word of web text (the training pool) | 2.03 | 3.04 | 1.69 | 1.36 |
| unknown-piece rate ↓ | 0.00 % | 0.68 % | 0.00 % | 0.00 % |
| words written without an unknown piece ↑ | 100.0 % | 94.5 % | 100.0 % | 100.0 % |
| text given back exactly after encode → decode: reference answers, character overlap (chrF, 0–100) ↑ | 100.0 | 91.1 | 100.0 | 100.0 |
| the same with the answers' diacritics removed first ↑ | 100.0 | 99.0 | 100.0 | 100.0 |
| single words given back exactly (of 2 000 corpus words) ↑ | 100.0 % | 99.3 % | 100.0 % | 100.0 % |
| roots kept inside one piece, where possible ↑ (root conservation, attainable) | 0.029 | 0.418 | 0.059 | 0.174 |
| share of words whose root can be kept at all (the ceiling) | 88.5 % | 88.5 % | 88.1 % | 88.5 % |
| pieces per morpheme (≈ 1 = cut at morpheme size; > 1 = cut finer) | 1.81 | 2.98 | 1.31 | 1.06 |
| the letter أ written as a choice answer, in pieces | 1 | 3 | 1 | 1 |
| pieces the adaptation never showed the model (stages 1–2) | not applicable (no new pieces) | 4.9 % | 3.1 % | 1.0 % |
| pieces it showed fewer than ten times | not applicable (no new pieces) | 20.3 % | 0.6 % | 3.9 % |

**What it shows.** How differently the four tokenizers cut the same Arabic text. A larger vocabulary cuts words into fewer, longer pieces; AraRooPat cuts every word into a root and a pattern, so it needs more pieces per word.

- AraRooPat's root conservation is high *by construction* on the words it writes as root + pattern; the number is a property of its design, not a measured skill (docs/report.md, the intrinsic metrics).
- A larger vocabulary trained on the same text sees each of its pieces less often during the model's adaptation; the last two rows say how many pieces the two adaptation stages never showed the model, or showed it fewer than ten times (scripts/count_adaptation_tokens.py, over the blocks the stages consumed).
- The native vocabularies are much larger than the from-scratch ones (see the first row); BPE-128K is the from-scratch tokenizer of native size.

*Source:* outputs/experiments/_comparative_tables/m5/tokenizer_basics.json (scripts/measure_tokenizer_basics.py) and each arm's intrinsic_metrics.json (the pipeline's intrinsic step)

- The native model needs no stages 1 and 2: its vocabulary is the one it was pretrained with.
- Equal compute is not equal text: the same 131 M pieces cover very different amounts of Arabic under different tokenizers (the two 'words' rows).
- Peak memory was not recorded for the Qwen3-4B runs; the Llama and Gemma runs record it (chains/*peak_mem.jsonl).

*Source:* google/gemma-3-4b-pt text config (resolved) + text-model parameters counted on the meta device (vision tower excluded); outputs/experiments/_comparative_tables/m5/tokenizer_basics.json; each arm's all_metrics.json (training wall times) and config.json (training budgets)
